Opakapaka selectivity: double-normal and double Richards

Introduction

This example compares the existing SS3 pattern-24 double-normal selectivity with the six-parameter double Richards curve for the ResFish fleet in the bundled opakapaka assessment. Both models retain the commercial logistic selectivity, use the same data and likelihoods, and estimate the same selectivity parameters. This is an illustrative curve-family comparison, not an assessment recommendation or an evaluation of parameter identifiability.

The double Richards curve has an ascending and descending generalized-logistic limb. Its six real-line parameters respectively control the ascending 50% point, ascending width, ascending shape, separation to the descending 50% point, descending width, and descending shape. Shape parameters of zero give logistic limbs. Unlike the double-normal curve, the double Richards curve is smooth in both length and its parameters. Its raw peak is not rescaled, so overlapping limbs can produce a peak below one.

Each fitted assessment is retained as an opal_fit S3 object. opal_fit stores portable model inputs, fitted parameters, bounds, optimization output, and diagnostics, while opal_fit_report() rebuilds or retrieves the session-specific RTMB objective only when a report is needed.

Packages and data 

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(opal)
library(RTMB)

data(opaka_data)
data(opaka_lf)
data(opaka_parameters)

data_base <- opaka_data
data_base$n_index <- 2L
data_base$priors <- NULL
data_base$A1 <- 0
data_base$A2 <- data_base$A1 + data_base$n_age - 1
data_base$min_age <- 0
data_base$age_a <- seq(data_base$min_age, by = 1, length.out = data_base$n_age)
data_base$sex_ratio <- rep(1, data_base$n_age)

lf_wide <- opaka_lf |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(fishery, year, month, ts),
              names_from = bin, values_from = value, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(fishery, ts)
data_base <- prep_lf_data(
  data_base, lf_wide, lf_keep_fisheries = c(1, 3),
  lf_var_adjust = rep(1, data_base$n_fishery), lf_addtocomp = 1e-10
)
data_base$lf_switch <- 1L
data_base$init_bias_adj_a <- get_bias_adj_vector(
  1949 - (data_base$age_a - 1), 1, c(1931, 1974, 2021.88, 2022.43), 0.869
)
data_base$bias_adj_y <- get_bias_adj_vector(
  (1949 - 1) + data_base$years, 1, c(1931, 1974, 2021.88, 2022.43), 0.869
)
data_base$sel_type_f <- c(1, 1, 2)

Paired model setup

SS3 parameters are converted before changing the ResFish type because the double Richards curve has no SS3 equivalent. The Richards starting values are obtained by fitting its curve to the converted double-normal curve on the length grid. This makes the comparison begin from similar selectivity shapes.

init_rdev_a <- rep(0, data_base$n_age)
init_rdev_a[1] <- opaka_parameters$rdev_y[1]
rdev_y <- c(opaka_parameters$rdev_y[-1], 0)

parameters_base <- list(
  log_B0 = 9,
  log_h = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_h),
  log_sigma_r = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_sigma_r),
  log_cpue_q = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_cpue_q),
  cpue_creep = as.numeric(rep(opaka_parameters$cpue_creep, data_base$n_index)),
  log_cpue_tau = rep(log(0.1), data_base$n_index),
  log_cpue_omega = as.numeric(rep(opaka_parameters$log_cpue_omega, data_base$n_index)),
  log_lf_tau = rep(log(0.1), data_base$n_fishery),
  log_L1 = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_L1),
  log_L2 = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_L2),
  log_k = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_k),
  log_CV1 = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_CV1),
  log_CV2 = as.numeric(opaka_parameters$log_CV2),
  par_sel = convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb(
    as.matrix(opaka_parameters$par_sel), data_base$sel_type_f, data_base$len_mid
  ),
  log_init_F_f = c(log(0.0119122), rep(log(1e-8), data_base$n_fishery - 1)),
  rdev_y = rdev_y,
  init_rdev_a = init_rdev_a
)

fit_richards_start <- MakeADFun(
  function(par) sum((
    sel_double_richards(data_base$len_mid, par) -
      sel_double_normal(data_base$len_mid, parameters_base$par_sel[3, ])
  )^2),
  c(parameters_base$par_sel[3, 1], 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)
)
richards_start <- nlminb(
  fit_richards_start$par, fit_richards_start$fn, fit_richards_start$gr,
  lower = rep(-5, 6), upper = rep(5, 6)
)$par

data_dn <- data_base
parameters_dn <- parameters_base

data_dr <- data_base
data_dr$sel_type_f[3] <- 3L
parameters_dr <- parameters_base
parameters_dr$par_sel[3, ] <- richards_start

For a fair structural comparison, both fits estimate the two commercial logistic parameters and all six ResFish selectivity parameters. Other parameters follow the opakapaka length-composition configuration.

make_map <- function(parameters, data) {
  selectivity_map <- matrix(NA_integer_, nrow(parameters$par_sel), ncol(parameters$par_sel))
  selectivity_map[1, 1:2] <- 1:2
  selectivity_map[3, ] <- 3:8
  list(
    log_h = factor(NA), log_sigma_r = factor(NA),
    cpue_creep = factor(rep(NA, data$n_index)),
    log_cpue_tau = factor(rep(NA, data$n_index)),
    log_cpue_omega = factor(rep(NA, data$n_index)),
    log_lf_tau = factor(rep(NA, length(parameters$log_lf_tau))),
    log_L1 = factor(NA), log_L2 = factor(NA), log_k = factor(NA),
    log_CV1 = factor(NA), log_CV2 = factor(NA),
    par_sel = factor(as.vector(selectivity_map)),
    log_init_F_f = factor(rep(NA, data$n_fishery)),
    init_rdev_a = factor(seq_len(data$n_age)),
    rdev_y = factor(seq_len(length(parameters$rdev_y)))
  )
}

fit_model <- function(data, parameters, selectivity) {
  data$priors <- get_priors(parameters, data)
  map <- make_map(parameters, data)
  obj <- MakeADFun(cmb(opal_model, data), parameters, map = map, silent = TRUE)
  bounds <- get_bounds(obj, parameters)
  lower <- bounds$lower
  upper <- bounds$upper
  control <- list(eval.max = 10000, iter.max = 10000)
  opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, lower = lower, upper = upper, control = control)
  opt <- nlminb(opt$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, lower = lower, upper = upper, control = control)
  opal_fit(
    data = data, obj = obj, opt = opt,
    bounds = list(lower = lower, upper = upper), control = control,
    estimability = tryCatch(check_estimability(obj = obj), error = identity),
    diagnostics = list(
      max_gradient = max(abs(obj$gr(opt$par))),
      high_correlations = tryCatch(
        get_cor_pairs(obj, threshold = 0.95), error = conditionMessage
      )
    ),
    metadata = list(selectivity = selectivity)
  )
}

fit_dn <- fit_model(data_dn, parameters_dn, "double_normal")
fit_dr <- fit_model(data_dr, parameters_dr, "double_richards")
report_dn <- opal_fit_report(fit_dn)
report_dr <- opal_fit_report(fit_dr)

data.frame(
  model = c("Double-normal", "Double Richards"),
  convergence = c(fit_dn$fit$opt$convergence, fit_dr$fit$opt$convergence),
  maximum_gradient = c(fit_dn$fit$diagnostics$max_gradient,
                       fit_dr$fit$diagnostics$max_gradient),
  nll = c(fit_dn$fit$opt$objective, fit_dr$fit$opt$objective)
)
fit_dn$fit[c("estimability", "diagnostics")]
fit_dr$fit[c("estimability", "diagnostics")]

Selectivity comparison

The curves below are raw selectivity. In particular, the double Richards maximum is informative: a value below one reflects overlap between its limbs and is not a normalization error.

par_dn <- fit_dn$parameters$par_sel[3, ]
par_dr <- fit_dr$parameters$par_sel[3, ]
selectivity_length <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(length = data_base$len_mid,
             selectivity = sel_double_normal(data_base$len_mid, par_dn),
             model = "Double-normal"),
  data.frame(length = data_base$len_mid,
             selectivity = sel_double_richards(data_base$len_mid, par_dr),
             model = "Double Richards")
)
ggplot(selectivity_length, aes(length, selectivity, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Length (cm)", y = "Raw selectivity", colour = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_bw()
natural <- double_richards_natural(data_base$len_mid, par_dr)
data.frame(parameter = names(natural), value = unname(natural))

l50_asc and l50_desc are directly interpretable 50% points. The widths equal a logistic 50-to-95% width only when their associated shape is one (par[3] or par[6] equals zero); otherwise they scale inverse steepness.

selectivity_age <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(age = data_base$age_a, selectivity = report_dn$sel_fya[3, 1, ],
             model = "Double-normal"),
  data.frame(age = data_base$age_a, selectivity = report_dr$sel_fya[3, 1, ],
             model = "Double Richards")
)
ggplot(selectivity_age, aes(age, selectivity, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Selectivity", colour = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_bw()

Fits and population consequences

The fitted length compositions are compared for ResFish observations. The models share the same observations; only their selectivity family differs.

composition_data <- function(fit, model) {
  index <- which(fit$data$lf_fishery_f == 3L)
  predicted <- opal_fit_report(fit)$lf_pred[[index]]
  observed <- fit$data$lf_obs_in[fit$data$lf_fishery == 3L, , drop = FALSE]
  observed <- observed / rowSums(observed)
  bind_rows(
    data.frame(year = rep(fit$data$lf_year[fit$data$lf_fishery == 3L], each = ncol(predicted)),
               length = rep(fit$data$len_mid, times = nrow(predicted)),
               value = as.vector(t(observed)), series = "Observed", model = model),
    data.frame(year = rep(fit$data$lf_year[fit$data$lf_fishery == 3L], each = ncol(predicted)),
               length = rep(fit$data$len_mid, times = nrow(predicted)),
               value = as.vector(t(predicted)), series = "Fitted", model = model)
  )
}
composition <- bind_rows(
  composition_data(fit_dn, "Double-normal"),
  composition_data(fit_dr, "Double Richards")
)
ggplot(composition, aes(length, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(model ~ year) +
  labs(x = "Length (cm)", y = "Proportion", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
component_sum <- function(report, component) sum(report[[component]])
fit_summary <- data.frame(
  model = c("Double-normal", "Double Richards"),
  nll = c(fit_dn$fit$opt$objective, fit_dr$fit$opt$objective),
  cpue_nll = c(component_sum(report_dn, "lp_cpue"), component_sum(report_dr, "lp_cpue")),
  length_nll = c(component_sum(report_dn, "lp_lf"), component_sum(report_dr, "lp_lf")),
  terminal_spawning_biomass = c(tail(report_dn$spawning_biomass_y, 1),
                                tail(report_dr$spawning_biomass_y, 1))
)
fit_summary

biomass <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(year = (1949 - 1) + c(data_base$years, max(data_base$years)+1),
             spawning_biomass = report_dn$spawning_biomass_y,
             model = "Double-normal"),
  data.frame(year = (1949 - 1) + c(data_base$years, max(data_base$years)+1),
             spawning_biomass = report_dr$spawning_biomass_y,
             model = "Double Richards")
)
ggplot(biomass, aes(year, spawning_biomass, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Spawning biomass", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

Use convergence status, gradients, check_estimability(), and get_cor_pairs() before drawing inferential conclusions. The flexible shape parameters can be weakly identified by real composition data, so this comparison should be accompanied by sensitivity analyses and uncertainty estimation before adopting double Richards selectivity in an assessment.
